questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Selective use of evidence
questions.learningObjective: Identify when a writer selects only supporting evidence
questions.stem: A city planner's memo cites three studies favoring a zoning change and omits two studies against it; what flaw does this show?

options.text: The memo commits cherry-picking by presenting only evidence that supports the proposed zoning change
The memo is valid because all cited studies are peer-reviewed and recent
options.misconception: confuses source quality with selection balance

options.text: The memo should include every study ever written on zoning
options.misconception: demands exhaustive rather than representative evidence

options.text: The memo commits no flaw because planners may choose their sources
options.misconception: treats editorial freedom as freedom from bias

questions.explanation: The memo selects only favorable studies, which is cherry-picking; quality of sources does not fix an unbalanced selection. Including every study is unnecessary, but balance is required.
questions.hint: Look for one-sided selection of evidence.

questions.explanation: The memo uses density in two distinct senses, physical and social; failing to notice the shift leads readers to import the wrong meaning. Context clues in each paragraph signal the active sense.
questions.hint: Check which sense fits each paragraph.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Who must show what
questions.learningObjective: Assign the burden of proof between parties

stimulus.body: The planning department claims a new bridge will reduce commute times by twenty percent. The neighborhood group disputes this. The department has the traffic models; the group has only anecdotes.

options.text: The planning department must support its own twenty percent claim
Both sides must prove their positions to the same standard
No one needs proof because the claim is only a projection
options.misconception: treats projections as exempt from support

questions.explanation: The party making the claim bears the burden of supporting it; the department owns the models and the assertion. The group need only raise doubt, not disprove with models.
